label: Convexity
notes: This opening chapter, printed pages 1 through 16, lays the combinatorial foundation of discrete geometry. We move from the definition of a convex set, through the convex hull, to the four pillars: Caratheodory, Radon, Helly, and the centerpoint theorem, each describing how finitely many points or sets in dimension d interlock.

label: Convex Sets and Affine Hulls
notes: A set is convex when every segment between two of its points stays inside. We contrast that with affine subspaces, the flat solution sets that are closed under all affine combinations. Affine independence of d plus one points fixes the dimension count that governs every theorem in the chapter.

label: The Convex Hull
notes: The convex hull is the smallest convex set containing X, equivalently the set of all convex combinations of points of X. We picture it as the rubber band snapped around a point cloud, and we note that in the plane its boundary is a convex polygon whose vertices are extreme points.

label: Caratheodory's Theorem
notes: Caratheodory bounds representation length: any point of the convex hull in R^d is already a convex combination of at most d plus one of the points. The proof reduces an overlong combination by following a direction in the kernel of an affine dependence, driving one coefficient to zero without leaving the hull.

label: Caratheodory Visualized
notes: In the plane d plus one equals three, so every interior point of the hull sits inside some triangle spanned by three sample points. The diagram triangulates the hull around the query point, making the bound concrete: three vertices always suffice, never more, to certify membership in the convex hull.

label: Radon's Lemma
notes: Radon's lemma states that any d plus two points in R^d can be split into two disjoint groups whose convex hulls intersect. The proof solves a homogeneous affine system, then sorts indices by the sign of the coefficients, building the shared point from the positive and negative parts of the dependence.

label: Radon Partition Visualized
notes: With four points in the plane, d plus two equals four, a Radon partition always exists. Either one point lies inside the triangle of the other three, or the two diagonals of a convex quadrilateral cross. The colored partition shows the two hulls overlapping at a single shared crossing point.

label: Helly's Theorem
notes: Helly's theorem is the finite intersection principle of convex geometry: if every d plus one of finitely many convex sets in R^d share a common point, then all of them do. The inductive proof removes one set at a time and uses Radon's lemma to glue the witness points back together.

label: Helly Visualized
notes: Three convex sets in the plane that meet pairwise need not share a point, but Helly with d plus one equals three guarantees a common point once every triple intersects. The diagram shows three overlapping regions whose triple overlap is the shaded lens certifying the common intersection.

label: Separation by Hyperplanes
notes: Two disjoint convex sets, one of them compact, can be strictly separated by a hyperplane: a linear functional that is below a threshold on one set and above it on the other. Separation is the analytic engine behind duality, supporting hyperplanes, and the existence proofs of the selection theorems.

label: The Centerpoint Theorem
notes: A centerpoint of n points is a point so deep that every closed halfplane containing it also contains at least n over d plus one of the points. The centerpoint theorem guarantees one exists for any configuration; its proof applies Helly to the family of deep halfspaces.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: The four theorems form one circle of ideas: Radon proves Helly, Helly proves the centerpoint theorem, and Caratheodory controls representation length. Together with separation they supply the combinatorial toolkit reused throughout the book for selection theorems, ham-sandwich cuts, and bounds on intersection patterns of convex sets.
